title: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

slides.title: The Fertile Crescent
slides.text: The Fertile Crescent is the band of countries nestling in a crescent shape around the Syrian desert — today's Egypt, Israel, Lebanon, Syria, Jordan, Iraq and parts of Turkey and Iran. What makes it fertile is the rivers: the Nile in Egypt, the Euphrates and the Tigris in Mesopotamia, the 'land between two rivers'. It is the cradle of the early advanced civilisations, and the reason it matters for legal history is writing: hieroglyphics in Egypt and cuneiform in Mesopotamia, both before 3000 BC. Law becomes visible to us only where it is written down, so the history of written law begins here.

terms.def: The crescent of land around the Syrian desert — Egypt, Israel, Lebanon, Syria, Jordan, Iraq, parts of Turkey and Iran — made fertile by the Nile, Euphrates and Tigris. Cradle of the first advanced civilisations and of writing.
'The land between two rivers' — between the Euphrates and the Tigris, in today's Iraq.

cards.q: What is the 'Fertile Crescent', and why is it the place where the history of written law begins?
cards.a: The crescent-shaped band of countries around the Syrian desert — today's Egypt, Israel, Lebanon, Syria, Jordan, Iraq and parts of Turkey and Iran — made fertile by the Nile, the Euphrates and the Tigris. Writing was developed there before 3000 BC (hieroglyphics in Egypt, cuneiform in Mesopotamia), and law becomes visible to us only once it is written down.

slides.title: The Egyptian kingdom
slides.text: Upper and Lower Egypt were unified by King Menes in the 32nd century BC, and what follows is a long and continuous development of the state — three flourishing periods (Old, Middle and New Kingdom) separated by intermediate periods. From 525 BC (and definitively 341 BC) Egypt is part of the Persian Empire. Continuity is the point to hold on to: Egypt is the contrast case to Mesopotamia on the next slides.

slides.title: Egyptian law: many documents, no code
slides.text: A large number of wills, contracts, adoptions and other transactions have survived on papyrus, leather and other materials — the Papyrus Museum in Vienna holds one of the largest collections in the world. What has NOT been found is a law book or a textbook. So we know a great deal about individual Egyptian transactions and very little about Egyptian law as a system: a coherent account cannot be given on this source basis. This is a lesson about method as much as about Egypt — what survives decides what can be known.

cards.q: Why can no coherent account of Egyptian law be given, despite abundant sources?
cards.a: Because what survived are individual transactions — wills, contracts, adoptions on papyrus and leather — and no law book or textbook has ever been found. We can see Egyptian legal practice but not the system behind it.

slides.title: The Mesopotamian kingdoms
slides.text: The opposite of Egypt: no steady development. Empires formed alternately in the north (Assyria) and in the south (Babylonia). In 539 BC Mesopotamia becomes part of the Persian Empire. The name Babylon is still a byword for the extravagance supposedly typical of a metropolis — Bruegel's Tower of Babel on the slide is the afterlife of that reputation.

cards.q: How does the political development of Mesopotamia differ from Egypt's?
cards.a: Egypt had a long, continuous development of one state; Mesopotamia had no steady development at all — empires rose alternately in the north (Assyria) and the south (Babylonia). Both end up in the Persian Empire: Mesopotamia in 539 BC, Egypt in 525/341 BC.

slides.title: Mesopotamian law and the Code of Hammurabi
slides.text: Several legal records survive. The oldest is the Code of Ur-Nammu (23rd/21st centuries BC); the most famous by far is the Code of Hammurabi, 18th century BC, whose stele stands in the Louvre. Its best-known provision is § 196: 'If a man put out the eye of another man, his eye shall be put out' — the talion principle, which reappears as a guiding principle in Judaism and Christianity. What these texts ARE is genuinely debatable, and the exam likes the debate: statutory law? records of customary law? were the rules actually in force at the time, or is this royal self-presentation? No answer is settled — say that the essence is disputed and name the possibilities.

terms.def: Babylonian legal text of the 18th century BC, the longest and best-preserved from the ancient Near East. The stele is in the Louvre; § 196 states the talion principle.
'An eye for an eye' — punishment mirroring the injury. Stated in the Code of Hammurabi and taken up in the Hebrew Bible, hence in two world religions.
The oldest surviving Mesopotamian legal record, 23rd/21st centuries BC — older than Hammurabi.

cards.q: What is the Code of Hammurabi — when, where is it now, and what is its most famous provision?
cards.a: A Babylonian legal text of the 18th century BC, the longest and best-preserved from the ancient Near East. The stele stands in the Louvre. § 196: 'If a man put out the eye of another man, his eye shall be put out' — the talion principle, which also guides Judaism and Christianity.

cards.q: Which Mesopotamian legal record is older than the Code of Hammurabi?
cards.a: The Code of Ur-Nammu, 23rd/21st centuries BC. Hammurabi's is the most famous, not the oldest.

cards.q: Why is it disputed what the Mesopotamian 'codes' actually are?
cards.a: Because it is not clear whether they are statutory law, written records of existing customary law, or royal self-presentation — and whether the rules were in force at all. The essence is debatable and the exam expects the possibilities to be named rather than one answer asserted.

slides.title: Palestine
slides.text: Historic Palestine covers both today's State of Israel and the Palestinian Territories. The Israelites migrate from Egypt in the 14th century BC — the exodus under Moses is described at length in the Bible. The heyday is the kingdom of David and Solomon in the 11th/10th century BC; afterwards the kingdom falls apart. The Northern Kingdom is conquered by the Assyrians in 720 BC and its population mixes with others and disappears from history. The Southern Kingdom, Judah, is conquered in 587 BC by the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar — the First Temple is demolished and the Babylonian exile lasts 597–539 BC. In 539 BC a smaller part of the Jews returns, but the land is almost never sovereign again, only part of larger empires. In 70 AD the Romans destroy the Second Temple.

cards.q: Give the sequence from David's kingdom to the destruction of the Second Temple.
cards.a: Heyday under David and Solomon (11th/10th c. BC) → the kingdom splits → the Northern Kingdom falls to Assyria in 720 BC and its people disappear from history → Judah falls to Nebuchadnezzar in 587 BC, the First Temple is destroyed and the Babylonian exile runs 597–539 BC → a smaller part returns in 539 BC, rarely sovereign again → the Romans destroy the Second Temple in 70 AD.

slides.title: Biblical law
slides.text: The Hebrew Bible corresponds roughly to the Christians' Old Testament. Its Torah — 'the law', 10th/6th century BC — contains many legal provisions, and they fall into two classes that Jewish law keeps apart: precepts governing relations between people (mitzvot bein adam lehaveiro) and precepts governing the relationship between the individual and the Almighty (mitzvot bein adam lamakom). There are many parallels to other ancient laws and mutual influence is often probable — but not always; parallel content does not prove borrowing. Beside the written law stands an oral tradition, the 'oral Torah', gathered as the Mishnah, which is itself recorded in the Jerusalem Talmud (about 400 AD) and the Babylonian Talmud (about 500 AD). Jewish legal history has its own topic later in the course (Topic 5).

terms.def: 'The law' — the legal core of the Hebrew Bible, 10th/6th century BC, containing precepts both between people and between the individual and God.
The written record of the 'oral Torah', later itself elaborated in the Jerusalem Talmud (c. 400 AD) and the Babylonian Talmud (c. 500 AD).

cards.q: Into which two classes does the Torah divide its precepts?
cards.a: Precepts pertaining to relations between people (mitzvot bein adam lehaveiro) and precepts pertaining to the relationship between the individual and the Almighty (mitzvot bein adam lamakom).

cards.q: What is the Mishnah, and where was it recorded?
cards.a: The written form of the 'oral Torah' — the tradition standing beside the written law. It was recorded in the Jerusalem Talmud (about 400 AD) and the Babylonian Talmud (about 500 AD).

cards.q: Ancient laws often resemble one another. What does the lecture warn about that?
cards.a: That mutual influence is often probable but not always — parallel content is not proof of borrowing. Similar rules can arise independently from similar problems.

slides.title: Persians and Greeks
slides.text: From the 6th century BC the Persians built the largest empire the world had yet seen — about 40 per cent of the world's population — conquering Mesopotamia in 539 BC and Egypt in 341 BC. Their attempts to conquer Greece failed in 490 and again in 479 BC. And Greece is the structural contrast: it was not a political entity at all but a multitude of city-states, the poleis — Athens, Sparta and many more. That fragmentation is exactly why there is no single 'Greek law'.

terms.def: The Greek city-state. Greece was a multitude of them, each with its own law — which is why there is no single ancient Greek legal order.

cards.q: Why is there no such thing as 'the' ancient Greek law?
cards.a: Because Greece was never a political entity, only a multitude of city-states (poleis) such as Athens and Sparta, each with its own law.

slides.title: Aristotle's forms of government
slides.text: A two-by-three table that has organised European constitutional thought ever since. The columns ask in whose interest rule is exercised: the common interest, or only the ruler's own. The rows ask how many rule. One person: monarchia in the common interest, tyrannis for himself. A few: aristokratia against oligarchia. Many: politeia against demokratia. Note the sting — for Aristotle demokratia is the DEGENERATE form of rule by many, the good form being politeia. The modern positive sense of 'democracy' is a later reversal, and the course returns to it when it reaches the Austrian constitution.

terms.def: In Aristotle's scheme the GOOD form of rule by many — in the common interest. Its degenerate counterpart is demokratia.

cards.q: Reproduce Aristotle's six forms of government.
cards.a: Rule by one: monarchia (common interest) / tyrannis (own interest). Rule by a few: aristokratia / oligarchia. Rule by many: politeia / demokratia. The left column serves the common interest, the right only the rulers themselves.

cards.q: What is surprising about the place of 'demokratia' in Aristotle's scheme?
cards.a: It is the degenerate form of rule by many — the good form is politeia. The modern positive sense of democracy is a later reversal of Aristotle's usage.

slides.title: Greek law: Athens and Gortyn
slides.text: Each polis had its own law, and only two are well studied, because only for those two is the source situation good enough: Athens and Gortyn on Crete. The Law of Gortyn (5th century BC) supplies the slide's example, and it shows how status passed: if a slave went to a free woman and wed her, the children were free; if a free woman went to a slave, the children were slaves. The rule turns on WHO went to WHOM — on the household in which the union took place — not on the mother's status as such.

cards.q: Which two ancient Greek legal orders are well studied, and why only those?
cards.a: Athens and Gortyn on Crete — because only for them is the surviving source material sufficient. Every polis had its own law; most of it is lost.

cards.q: Under the Law of Gortyn, were the children of a slave and a free woman free?
cards.a: It depended on which way the union went: if the slave came to the free woman and wed her, the children were free; if the free woman went to the slave, the children were slaves.

slides.title: Slavery in antiquity
slides.text: There is no consistent terminology, and the differences inside the category are large: between female and male slaves, and according to the type of use — doctors, teachers, farmers, miners. Slaves were subject to the house father, in part like other members of the household. The legal-historical point comes last: it was ROMAN law that first established a comprehensive body of rules governing slavery. Before that, slavery is a social fact with scattered legal consequences rather than a legal institution.

cards.q: What did Roman law add to ancient slavery?
cards.a: The first comprehensive set of legal rules governing it. Earlier antiquity had no consistent terminology and treated slaves very differently by sex and by use (doctors, teachers, farmers, miners), under the authority of the house father.

slides.title: Alexander and Hellenism
slides.text: Alexander of Macedonia conquers the Persian Empire; after his death it breaks into several kingdoms, of which the most important are the Ptolemaic Empire in Egypt and the Seleucid Empire in Syria. Hellenism is the fusion that follows: Greek and Persian culture merging with the culture of the Fertile Crescent. But — and this is the legal-historical point — no uniform legal order came out of it. Cultural fusion did not produce legal unification; that had to wait for Rome.

terms.def: The fusion of Greek and Persian culture with that of the Fertile Crescent after Alexander's conquests. Cultural, not legal: it produced no uniform legal order.

cards.q: What did Hellenism achieve culturally, and what did it NOT achieve legally?
cards.a: It fused Greek and Persian culture with that of the Fertile Crescent across the kingdoms that succeeded Alexander (chiefly Ptolemaic Egypt and Seleucid Syria). It produced no uniform legal order — legal unification of the Mediterranean came only with Rome.

slides.title: The Mediterranean world in the 3rd century BC
slides.text: The map shows the powers before Rome absorbs them: Rome with the League of Corinth, Carthage, Macedon, the Seleucid Empire, the Ptolemaic Empire, Armenia.

slides.title: Why Roman law matters for European legal culture
slides.text: Five steps, and they are the spine of the whole course. Roman law was the law of the entire Mediterranean world in antiquity. It was 'rediscovered' in the Middle Ages. It was 'received' in the modern age. It remained IN FORCE in Austria until 31 December 1811 — that is, until the ABGB entered into force on 1 January 1812. And Roman legal thought and Roman legal concepts continue to shape European legal culture to this day. Note the disclaimer: the CONTENT of Roman law is a separate subject; this lecture deals only with its effects on European legal culture.

terms.def: The taking-over of Roman law into the legal orders of the modern age, following its medieval 'rediscovery'. Treated in detail in the topic on the ius commune.

cards.q: Until when was Roman law in force in Austria?
cards.a: Until 31 December 1811 — it was displaced by the ABGB, which entered into force on 1 January 1812.

cards.q: Trace the significance of Roman law for European legal culture in steps.
cards.a: Law of the whole Mediterranean world in antiquity → 'rediscovered' in the Middle Ages → 'received' in the modern age → in force in Austria until 31 December 1811 → its concepts and its way of thinking still shape European legal culture today.

slides.title: The Roman Republic and the praetor
slides.text: 510 BC (the date is uncertain) is taken as the beginning of the Roman Republic. Political power lies with the Senate, and two consuls head the executive. In 367 BC the praetor is created to relieve the consuls: he heads the judiciary — and note who these men were, because the exam does: POLITICIANS, not jurists. In 27 BC Octavian, as Augustus, becomes the first imperator and turns the Republic into an empire while KEEPING the offices and structures of the Republic. He rejects the title of king and calls himself princeps senatus, the first of the senate — hence the name of the period, the principate, 27 BC to 284 AD. The office of praetor survives into the 6th century AD.

terms.def: Roman magistrate created in 367 BC to relieve the consuls; head of the judiciary. A politician, not a jurist — he relied on the responsa of jurists.
27 BC–284 AD: rule by the emperor as princeps senatus, 'first of the senate', with the republican offices and structures formally retained.

cards.q: Who was the praetor, when was the office created, and what is the catch about who held it?
cards.a: The head of the Roman judiciary, created in 367 BC to relieve the consuls. The catch: praetors were politicians, not jurists — the legal expertise came from the jurists who advised them.

cards.q: How did Augustus change the Roman constitution in 27 BC, and why is the period called the 'principate'?
cards.a: He became the first imperator and turned the Republic into an empire while retaining the republican offices and structures. He refused the title of king and styled himself princeps senatus, 'first of the senate' — hence principate, 27 BC to 284 AD.

slides.title: The Roman jurists
slides.text: The decisive structural fact about Roman law: it was primarily JURISPRUDENTIAL law — case law made by jurists, only supplemented at first by acts of legislation. The 'responsa jurists' gave expert opinions in civil proceedings, both to the parties (consilia) and to the praetor (responsa). The first jurists were priests; later they were other wealthy Romans who did not work for money but dealt with legal problems out of interest and inclination. The slide's aside is worth keeping: Cicero was a LAWYER, not a jurist — an advocate who argued cases, not one of the learned men whose opinions made law.

terms.def: Expert opinions given by Roman jurists to the praetor; opinions given to the parties were consilia. The mechanism by which jurists' learning became law.

cards.q: What kind of legal source was Roman law primarily, and who made it?
cards.a: Jurisprudential law — case law made by jurists, at first only supplemented by legislation. Jurists gave expert opinions to the parties (consilia) and to the praetor (responsa); the first were priests, later wealthy Romans who worked without payment, out of interest.

cards.q: Why is Cicero described as 'a lawyer, not a jurist'?
cards.a: He argued cases as an advocate. A jurist in the Roman sense was one of the learned men whose opinions (responsa, consilia) were themselves a source of law.

slides.title: Classical Roman jurisprudence and the law of citation
slides.text: The classical age of Roman jurisprudence is divided into the early classical age (1st century AD), the peak (2nd century) and the late classical age (3rd century). Law schools emerge — the Sabinians against the Proculians. And then the problem of abundance: there were too many jurists with too many conflicting opinions, so in 426 the emperor ordered that only the doctrines of SIX jurists were legally binding. That is the 'law of citation', and it is the moment authority is rationed by statute because jurisprudence had become unmanageable.

terms.def: Imperial order that only the doctrines of six named jurists were legally binding — a response to the unmanageable mass of conflicting juristic opinion.

cards.q: What was the 'law of citation' of 426, and what problem was it solving?
cards.a: An imperial order that only the doctrines of six jurists were legally binding. The problem was abundance: too many jurists with too many conflicting opinions had made jurisprudential law unmanageable.

cards.q: How is classical Roman jurisprudence periodised?
cards.a: Early classical age — 1st century AD; peak of the classical age — 2nd century; late classical age — 3rd century. Law schools of the period: the Sabinians and the Proculians.

slides.title: Roman statutory law
slides.text: The Twelve Tables of 451 BC count as the beginning of Roman law. The principle that governs everything after them: legislative acts should only SUPPLEMENT jurisprudential law, not replace it. Examples: the Lex Aquilia (286 BC), the Lex Iulia (18 BC), and much later the Codex Theodosianus of 438 AD. The Twelve Tables are carved on the building of the German Federal Administrative Court in Leipzig as a counterpart to the Ten Commandments opposite — law from reason facing law from revelation.

terms.def: 451 BC, taken as the beginning of Roman law. The first written statement of Roman statutory law.

cards.q: What marks the beginning of Roman law, and what was the relationship between Roman statute and jurisprudence?
cards.a: The Twelve Tables, 451 BC. Legislation was meant only to supplement jurisprudential law, never to replace it — examples are the Lex Aquilia (286 BC), the Lex Iulia (18 BC) and the Codex Theodosianus (438 AD).

slides.title: From the principate to the dominate
slides.text: The main weakness of the principate was that succession was never settled: inheritance, adoption, but mostly military strength decided who ruled. In the 3rd century the empire falls into deep crisis, resolved for a time by Diocletian (284–305 AD). His answer is collegial imperial government: two Augusti and two Caesars as their designated successors, with the empire divided into four tetrarchies for administrative purposes. In the long run one emperor emerges in the west and one in the east — while the IDEA of the unity of the empire is retained for a long time afterwards.

terms.def: Diocletian's arrangement: two Augusti and two Caesars as successors, with the empire divided into four administrative parts — an answer to the unsolved problem of imperial succession.

cards.q: What was the chronic weakness of the principate, and how did Diocletian answer it?
cards.a: Succession was never regulated — inheritance, adoption, but mostly military strength decided. Diocletian (284–305) introduced collegial rule: two Augusti and two Caesars as designated successors, with four administrative tetrarchies.

slides.title: The Roman Empire, divided 395
slides.text: The division of 395 AD, which the introductory lecture used for the genealogy of the imperial title.

slides.title: Christianity
slides.text: Jesus Christ preaches in Palestine around 30 AD and is executed by the Roman occupation forces; his followers hold on to him. The orally transmitted teachings are written down from about 60 AD — the 'New Testament' supplements the 'Old Testament', the Jewish Bible, and it too contains many legal provisions, for instance the indivisibility of marriage. Christianity is originally rooted in Judaism and separates from it only gradually, especially after 70 AD. The Romans refuse it recognition and persecute Christians several times until 311/313 AD; in 380 Christianity becomes the STATE RELIGION of the Roman Empire. Two dates to keep apart: 311/313 is toleration, 380 is establishment.

cards.q: Distinguish what happened to Christianity in 311/313 and in 380.
cards.a: 311/313: the persecutions end and Christianity is tolerated. 380: Christianity becomes the state religion of the Roman Empire. Toleration and establishment are two different steps, roughly seventy years apart.

cards.q: Does the New Testament contain legal provisions?
cards.a: Yes — it supplements the Old Testament and carries legal content of its own, for example the indivisibility of marriage. It was written down from about 60 AD.

slides.title: The church splits
slides.text: In the 4th and 5th centuries serious conflicts of faith arise around the person of Jesus Christ — God and human in one person? The councils of 431 and 451 are meant to resolve them, and they reject both extreme positions: the Copts in Egypt and the Nestorians in the Near East are excluded. The consequence is political as well as religious: suppression by the Roman imperial church on one side and tolerance by Muslims on the other made the transfer of power to the Muslims in Egypt and the Near East in the 7th century easier. The Roman imperial church kept unity of faith — its later disintegration into a Latin and a Greek church happened for POLITICAL, not theological reasons.

cards.q: What did the councils of 431 and 451 decide, and what political consequence did the lecture draw from it?
cards.a: They rejected both extreme positions on the nature of Christ, excluding the Copts in Egypt and the Nestorians in the Near East. Suppressed by the imperial church and tolerated by Muslims, those communities made the 7th-century transfer of power to the Muslims in Egypt and the Near East easier.

cards.q: Was the split between the Latin and the Greek church theological?
cards.a: No. The Roman imperial church kept unity of faith; the disintegration into a Latin and a Greek church happened for political reasons.

slides.title: The Migration Period (4th–6th century)
slides.text: The map of the peoples on the move: Saxons, Franks, Alemanni, Bavarians, Visigoths, and the Vandals and Ostrogoths — the last two later defeated by Justinian.

slides.title: Justinian I (527–565)
slides.text: Emperor of the Eastern Roman — Byzantine — Empire, and a reformer on a large scale. He attempted to reconquer the Western Roman Empire, without lasting success. What did last is the compilation of classical Roman law in the Corpus Iuris Civilis, 529/534. Everything Europe later 'rediscovered' of Roman law, it rediscovered through this compilation.

cards.q: Why does Justinian matter more for legal history than for political history?
cards.a: His reconquest of the Western Empire did not last, but his compilation of classical Roman law — the Corpus Iuris Civilis, 529/534 — did. It is the form in which Roman law reached medieval and modern Europe.

slides.title: The Corpus Iuris Civilis
slides.text: Four parts, and the exam expects them by name and function. CODEX: the collection of imperial laws (constitutiones), first version 529, second 534. DIGEST (Pandects): a collection of the writings of the classical jurists — chiefly Ulpian, Paulus and Papinian — published in 533, and INTERPOLATED, that is shortened and 'modernised', which from today's perspective means falsified. INSTITUTIONES: an authorised textbook, also 533. NOVELLAE: later supplements, which survive largely only in Greek. Two things to hold: the Digest preserves classical jurisprudence but not unaltered, and the Novellae are already a Greek-language world — the Corpus stands on the hinge between Latin antiquity and Byzantium.

terms.def: The part of the Corpus Iuris Civilis collecting the writings of the classical jurists (Ulpian, Paulus, Papinian), published 533 — interpolated, i.e. shortened and modernised by the compilers.
The compilers' alteration of classical juristic texts when assembling the Digest: shortening and 'modernising'. From today's standpoint, falsification of the sources.
The authorised textbook within the Corpus Iuris Civilis, published 533.

cards.q: Name the four parts of the Corpus Iuris Civilis and say what each contains.
cards.a: Codex — the imperial laws (constitutiones), 529, second version 534. Digest / Pandects — the writings of the classical jurists, chiefly Ulpian, Paulus and Papinian, 533. Institutiones — the authorised textbook, 533. Novellae — later supplements, surviving largely only in Greek.

cards.q: What does it mean that the Digest is 'interpolated', and why does it matter?
cards.a: The compilers shortened and 'modernised' the classical texts they collected — from today's standpoint, falsified them. It matters because the Digest is our main access to classical jurisprudence, and what it transmits is not the classical text unaltered.

slides.title: From Byzantium to modern Greek law
slides.text: After 534 Byzantine law develops in Greek: the Basilika, the 'imperial books', in 907; the Hexabiblos, the 'six books', in 1345; and finally the Greek Civil Code of 1946. A line of continuity from Justinian to the twentieth century, running outside the western reception.

cards.q: Name the stages from the Corpus Iuris Civilis to the modern Greek Civil Code.
cards.a: After 534 Byzantine law continues in Greek: the Basilika ('imperial books') in 907, the Hexabiblos ('six books') in 1345, and the Greek Civil Code of 1946.

slides.title: Islam
slides.text: The section on Islamic law opens with the Hagia Sophia in Istanbul, whose own history is the region's in miniature: church 537–1453, mosque 1453–1935, museum 1935–2020, mosque again since 2020.

cards.q: What has the Hagia Sophia been, and when?
cards.a: Church 537–1453, mosque 1453–1935, museum 1935–2020, and a mosque again since 2020.

slides.title: Muhammad and the rise of Islam
slides.text: Mecca was already a cultural and economic centre in pre-Islamic times — the Jahiliya — where pagans, Jews and Christians met. Muhammad preaches monotheism and has to flee to Medina on 16 July 622: the Hijra, from which the Islamic calendar counts. By Muhammad's death in 632 AD (11 AH) most of Arabia is Muslim. Under the 'rightly guided caliphs' the Fertile Crescent, Persia and North Africa are subjugated, and expansion continues to Spain and India. Early Islamic law therefore emerges in a trading society that already knew several religious laws, and it spreads with astonishing speed over the whole area this lecture began with.

terms.def: Muhammad's flight from Mecca to Medina on 16 July 622, the epoch of the Islamic calendar (AH = anno Hegirae).
The pre-Islamic period in Arabia. Mecca was already a cultural and economic centre where pagans, Jews and Christians met.

cards.q: When, where and how did early Islamic law emerge?
cards.a: In Arabia in the 7th century, in a trading society (Mecca in the Jahiliya) where pagans, Jews and Christians already met. Muhammad preached monotheism, fled to Medina on 16 July 622 (the Hijra, year 1 AH), and by his death in 632 (11 AH) most of Arabia was Muslim; under the 'rightly guided caliphs' the law spread over the Fertile Crescent, Persia, North Africa, then Spain and India.

cards.q: What is the Hijra and why does it matter for dating?
cards.a: Muhammad's flight from Mecca to Medina on 16 July 622. The Islamic calendar counts from it — 632 AD is 11 AH.

slides.title: Caliphs and imams: the Sunni–Shia split
slides.text: The problem is the succession to the Prophet. The first four successors — caliphs — come from his family circle: the Rashidun, the 'rightly guided' caliphate, 632–661. After the assassination of the fourth caliph, ʿAli, Muhammad's son-in-law, the Muslims divide. The SUNNI line runs on through the Umayyad caliphate in Damascus (661–750), the Abbasid caliphate in Baghdad (750–1258), a powerless Abbasid caliphate in Cairo (1261–1517), and the Ottoman caliphate in Constantinople (1517–1924). The SHIA line counts imams from ʿAli as the first through to the twelfth, Muhammad al-Mahdi, 'the hidden imam': the Minor Occultation in 874 and the Major Occultation in 941, after which the imam is held to return only at the end of the world. So the split is about legitimate succession, and it produces two different structures of authority — a caliph who rules, and an imam who is awaited.

terms.def: The 'rightly guided' caliphate, 632–661: the first four successors of Muhammad, from his family circle.
In Twelver Shia belief, the concealment of the twelfth imam, Muhammad al-Mahdi — Minor Occultation 874, Major Occultation 941. He is held to return only at the end of the world.

cards.q: What caused the split between Sunna and Shia?
cards.a: The question of legitimate succession to the Prophet. The first four caliphs came from his family circle (Rashidun, 632–661); after the assassination of the fourth, ʿAli, Muhammad's son-in-law, the community divided over who could rightfully succeed.

cards.q: Name the caliphates in order, with their seats.
cards.a: Rashidun 632–661; Umayyad in Damascus 661–750; Abbasid in Baghdad 750–1258; Abbasid in Cairo (powerless) 1261–1517; Ottoman in Constantinople 1517–1924.

cards.q: Who is the 'hidden imam' and what are the two Occultations?
cards.a: Muhammad al-Mahdi, the twelfth imam of the Shia line beginning with ʿAli. Minor Occultation 874, Major Occultation 941; he is held to return only at the end of the world.

slides.note: The slide's text layer has an extra 1 inserted into the dates ('1570–1632 Muhammad', '1750–1258 Abbasid'). The correct dates are 570–632 (Muhammad), 632–661 (Rashidun), 661–750 (Umayyads), 750–1258 (Abbasids in Baghdad). To be checked against the slide image.

slides.title: Is the sharia 'law' on this course's definition?
slides.text: The lecture deliberately turns its own definition back on the sharia. 'Law is a regulatory system which is created by humans for humans and is generally effective, and which may apply organized coercion.' Two frictions follow. First, some sharia norms originate — according to Islamic belief — directly from God, not from humans. Second, not all sharia norms apply organized coercion; many are religious or moral duties. So the definition does not fit without remainder, which is precisely why the distinction on the next slides matters: it is the task of fiqh to separate the legal from the moral norms.

cards.q: Where does the sharia strain the course's definition of law?
cards.a: At two points. The definition says law is created by humans, but some sharia norms are held to come directly from God. And it allows for organized coercion, whereas many sharia norms carry none — they are religious or moral duties. Separating the legal from the moral is the task of fiqh.

cards.q: Is the sharia only a legal order, or also a moral one?
cards.a: Also a moral one. It is considered both, and it is the task of fiqh — Islamic jurisprudence — to distinguish the legal norms within it from the moral ones.

slides.title: The five qualifications of the sharia
slides.text: Every act is placed in one of five classes: wājib, obligatory; mandūb (sunna), recommended; halal (mubāḥ), indifferent or permissible; makrūh, reprehensible; ḥarām, forbidden. Note the shape — it is a scale with a neutral middle, not a binary of permitted and forbidden, and the two middle classes (recommended, reprehensible) carry no coercion at all. That is the structural reason the sharia is a moral order as much as a legal one, and why fiqh has to sort the two.

terms.def: Islamic jurisprudence — the scholarly work of deriving and distinguishing norms, including telling legal norms from moral ones.

cards.q: Name the five qualifications the sharia gives to an act.
cards.a: wājib — obligatory; mandūb (sunna) — recommended; halal (mubāḥ) — indifferent or permissible; makrūh — reprehensible; ḥarām — forbidden.

cards.q: What does the five-fold scale show about the nature of the sharia?
cards.a: That it is not a binary of permitted and forbidden but a scale with a neutral middle, whose 'recommended' and 'reprehensible' classes carry no coercion. That is why the sharia is a moral as well as a legal order, and why fiqh must separate the two.

slides.title: Sources of the sharia
slides.text: Three sources are common to all: the Qurʾan, God's literal revelation to Muhammad; the Hadīth, transmitted reports about the Sunnah, that is the traditions and practices of Muhammad; and Ijtihad, independent reasoning. Sunni Muslims add Ijmāʿ, the consensus of authoritative Muslims. Shia Muslims add the Hadīth of the imams. The hierarchy is what the exam's al-Shafiʿi source turns on: a tradition going back to the Prophet is authoritative and can be displaced only by another authoritative tradition from the Prophet; where two are equally reliable, the one more in keeping with the Qurʾan and the undisputed sunna prevails; traditions from other persons count for nothing against a tradition from the Prophet. Al-Shafiʿi, who set that out, gives his name to the Shafiʿi school.

terms.def: God's literal revelation to Muhammad — the first source of the sharia.
Transmitted reports about the Sunnah, the traditions and practices of Muhammad.
Independent reasoning as a source of the sharia — the faculty whose 'gates' close in the 12th century and reopen in the 19th/20th.
Consensus among authoritative Muslims; a source recognised by Sunni Muslims.

cards.q: Name the sources of the sharia, and say which are common and which are not.
cards.a: Common to all: the Qurʾan (God's literal revelation), the Hadīth (reports about the Sunnah of Muhammad) and Ijtihad (independent reasoning). Sunnis add Ijmāʿ, the consensus of authoritative Muslims; Shia add the Hadīth of the imams.

cards.q: According to al-Shafiʿi, how do the sources rank against one another?
cards.a: A tradition from the Prophet related by reliable persons is authoritative and can be rejected only by another authoritative tradition from the Prophet. If two are equally reliable, the one more in keeping with the Qurʾan and the undisputed sunna prevails. Traditions from other persons count for nothing against a tradition from the Prophet.

cards.q: Who was al-Shafiʿi and which school of law goes back to him?
cards.a: An Islamic jurist of the 2nd century AH / 8th century AD who set out the ranking of the sources of the sharia. The Shafiʿi school (madhhab) is traced back to him; the other Sunni schools are the Hanafi, Maliki and Hanbali.

slides.title: The schools of fiqh (madhāhib)
slides.text: A map of where the schools of Islamic jurisprudence prevail. The four Sunni schools are the Hanafi, Maliki, Shafiʿi and Hanbali; the Shia have their own, chiefly the Jaʿfari. They differ not about the sources but about how far and by what means the sources may be reasoned from — which is exactly the question the next slide turns into a period division.

terms.def: A school of Islamic jurisprudence. The four Sunni schools are Hanafi, Maliki, Shafiʿi and Hanbali.

cards.q: Name the four Sunni schools of fiqh, and say what separates them.
cards.a: Hanafi, Maliki, Shafiʿi and Hanbali. They agree on the sources and differ over how far, and by what methods, one may reason from them.

slides.title: Peak and decline — the gates of Ijtihad
slides.text: The closing arc. In the 12th century the 'gates of Ijtihad' are said to close: independent reasoning gives way to following established doctrine. In 1258 the Mongols take Baghdad and the caliphate there ends. In the 16th century Egypt and Mesopotamia become part of the Ottoman Empire. In the 19th century European influence grows sharply — the 'export of law' to the Levant. And in the 19th and 20th centuries the gates of Ijtihad are declared open again. The slide's portrait is Ibn Rushd, latinised Averroes (1126–98), the Spanish-Muslim philosopher famous for his work on Aristotle: a reminder that at its height this culture was the route by which Greek philosophy returned to Europe.

terms.def: The metaphor for whether independent legal reasoning is permitted. Said to close in the 12th century in favour of following established doctrine, and to open again in the 19th/20th century.

cards.q: What does it mean that the 'gates of Ijtihad' closed, when did it happen, and when did they open again?
cards.a: That independent legal reasoning gave way to following established doctrine. They are said to have closed in the 12th century and to have opened again in the 19th/20th century.

cards.q: Give the stages of the decline of the classical Islamic legal culture.
cards.a: 12th century: the gates of Ijtihad close. 1258: the Mongols take Baghdad and the caliphate there ends. 16th century: Egypt and Mesopotamia become Ottoman. 19th century: growing European influence and the 'export of law' to the Levant. 19th/20th century: the gates of Ijtihad open again.

cards.q: Who was Ibn Rushd, and why does he appear in a legal history lecture?
cards.a: Averroes (1126–98), the Spanish-Muslim philosopher famous for his work on Aristotle. He stands for the moment when Islamic culture was the route by which Greek philosophy returned to Europe.
